posts.title: Painting rings on a spinning top
posts.excerpt: The rings on a koma are painted while it turns on the lathe: one steady hand, one small brush, three seconds a ring.
posts.content:
The rings on a koma are painted while it turns on the lathe. One steady hand, one small brush, three seconds a ring.

Red, black, red

We use three colours and never more: the red of a kendama ball, sumi black and the bare wood between them. When the top spins, the rings blur into one warm colour.

A wobbly ring is sanded off and painted again. A top is only as good as its slowest spin.

posts.title: Beech, cherry and a winter of drying
posts.excerpt: Every plank from the timber yard sits on our racks for a whole winter before it meets the lathe.
posts.content:
Every plank from the timber yard next door sits on our racks for a whole winter before it meets the lathe.

Why wait

Wet wood moves. A kendama cup turned too early turns oval by spring, and the ball no longer sits. So we stack the planks with spacers, turn them once a month and wait.

posts.title: Our table at the winter fair
posts.excerpt: Each December we carry two crates of toys to the craft fair by the river. Here is what is going in them.
posts.content:
Each December we carry two crates of toys to the craft fair by the river.

Under the lamp

Tops go at the front, where children can spin them on the table. Kendama hang from a rail at the back, with one left out for anyone who wants to try a catch.

posts.title: A hundred catches before the shelf
posts.excerpt: Before a kendama goes on the shelf, someone in the shop catches the ball on every cup a hundred times.
posts.content:
Before a kendama goes on the shelf, someone in the shop catches the ball on every cup a hundred times.

Listening

A good kendama sounds dry and short when the ball lands. A rattle means a loose cup or a hole drilled off-centre, and that kendama goes back to the lathe.
